                                       I.        Introduction and Summary
       This proceeding is unprecedented for many reasons. The Bell County East Switch to Big
Hill Substation 765-kilovolt (“kV”) transmission line project (“Project”) is one of the first, longest,
and most expensive 765-kV transmission lines proposed in the state. The Project will cost ratepay-
ers anywhere from $2.03 billion to $2.25 billion, condemn a 200' easement across Texas for be-
tween 214 miles and 244 miles, and directly impact 80 to 184 habitable structures (i.e., Texans’
homes, churches, schools, and businesses).
       Unsurprisingly, no one wants the Project on or near their land. 1 So this docket has, under-
standably, received great public interest—more than any certificate-of-convenience-and-necessity
(“CCN”) docket before it, including the most contentious of the 2009–2011 competitive-renewa-
ble-energy-zone (“CREZ”) transmission lines. 2 And this massive project, with its substantial land-
owner and ratepayer opposition, must be processed on an impossibly rushed schedule while facing
a looming 180-day statutory deadline, 3 which the Applicants refused to waive. 4
      In every CCN proceeding, the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) and the Public Utility
Commission of Texas (“Commission”) must, of course, ground their decisions in the text of PURA
and Commission rules.5 But in a proceeding like this—for a first-of-its-kind extra-high-voltage

statutory and regulatory factors. As former Commission Chair Barry Smitherman testified,
“[t]hat’s the only way to ensure that the process is legitimate, and we have to have a legitimate
process [for] landowners to accept what is happening to their property.” 6
        After reviewing the record in this proceeding, the M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Land-
owners do not dispute the Applicants’ conclusion that Route 894 best meets the statutory and reg-
ulatory routing factors. If the ALJs and the Commission first determine that the Applicants have
met their burden to demonstrate the need for the Project, 7 the M31, M32, and M33 Opposition

that Route 894 best meets the statutory and regulatory routing factors, the M31, M32, and M33
Opposition Landowners also do not oppose Routes 487 or 891.

                                          II.      Factual Background
       On March 26, 2026, Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Trans-
mission Services Corporation (“LCRA TSC”) (collectively, “Applicants”) filed a joint application
(“Application”) with the Commission to amend their respective CCNs to construct and maintain
the Project in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard,
Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson counties. 8
        The Project is a portion of the 765-kV import paths described in the Permian Basin Relia-
bility Plan. Specifically, the Project is the eastern segment of Import Path 2 and consists of (1) a
new 765-kV single-circuit transmission line between LCRA TSC’s Big Hill Substation and On-
cor’s Bell County East Switch and (2) an expansion of Oncor’s existing Bell County East Switch
to include a 765/345-kV station.
        The Applicants propose 122 alternative routes and 171 alternative route links. Of those 122
alternative routes, 21 routes include some combination of Links M31, M32, and M33. 9 Combined,
Links M31, M32, and M33 run consecutively for about 25 miles from the middle of northern

          None of these statutory and regulatory factors “is intended to be absolute in the sense that
any one shall prevail in all possible circumstances.” 41 And “no one factor controls or is disposi-
tive.” 42 Instead, the ALJs and Commission have “authority to consider and weigh a variety of
factors—engineering constraints, costs, grid reliability, and security, along with the criteria in
PURA [§] 37.056—in addition to the use of existing rights-of-way in determining the most rea-
sonable route for a transmission line.” 43
         As ALJs have consistently noted “[s]ome of the factors are inherently in conflict, and nei-
ther PURA nor Commission rules specify the relative weight to be given to each factor.” 44 So the
“Commission and the ALJs must consider the totality of all factors, even if individual factors—
considered in isolation—could lead to opposite outcomes.” 45

[routes that use filed links].” 47 Commission Staff’s role is “to provide an independent recommen-
dation based upon a review of the application and evidence provided in this proceeding.” 48 And

of residential and small commercial consumers.” 49 Of those three, the Applicants recommend
